items.title: Request: generic party actor records (customer, supplier, employee, custodian, market-segment, governance-stakeholder) — needed as served-party references by the value-stream catalog
items.body:
## Summary

CR-ACT-07 (first admission, seed records) proves the Phase-2 pipeline end-to-end. This issue requests the next admission tranche from the value-stream catalog's side: the **generic party actor records** that downstream catalogs need as referential served-party and stage-actor references.

## Requesting repo

`technehub-labs/dea-catalog-value-streams` — its records carry a `customer_ref` slot (served party) and per-stage `actor_refs` slots that have been deliberately unpopulated since its CR-VS-03 because this catalog did not yet carry these records, and fabricating references would violate the reference-resolution contract. The dependency is now formalized in [CR-VS-09](https://github.com/technehub-labs/dea-catalog-value-streams/blob/main/change-requests/CR-VS-09.md) (dependency-gated on exactly this admission).

## Requested records (with consumers)

| Generic party | Consuming value streams | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| customer | Order to Cash, Issue to Resolve, Contract to Renewal, Return to Credit | most-requested; external served party |
| supplier | Procure to Pay | trading-party counterpart |
| employee | Hire to Retire | internal served party |
| internal-asset-custodian | Acquire to Retire | internal operator/custodian |
| market-segment (or closest admitted form) | Concept to Launch | the "market" as served party |
| governance-stakeholder (or closest admitted form) | Plan to Forecast, Record to Report | oversight stakeholders |

Naming and granularity are yours to decide per your research method — CR-VS-09 §3 records that if the actors catalog admits different granularity (e.g. a generic `external-party`), the value-stream side revises its mapping table at execution time rather than the streams' semantics. The value-stream backfill consumes whatever ids you admit; its referential-integrity gate enforces resolution, so nothing can land with invented ids.

## Suggested method

Treat the six party archetypes as candidate seeds in your own research pipeline (candidate universe → evidence → admission), rather than a bulk-authoring request. The value-stream catalog's evidence register (SRC-001 BIZBOK value-stream guidance, SRC-003 stakeholder-value observations) is available as cross-catalog evidence input if useful.

## Consumer-side status

- Schema support: `customer_ref` (stream-level) and `actor_refs` (per-stage) already exist in the value-stream entry schema (CR-VS-07).
- Referential-integrity gate: the `actors:` namespace is already wired and will activate automatically as soon as any `actors:` ref is populated (resolution: clone → CATALOG.yaml index → vendored snapshot).
- Execution plan: [CR-VS-09](https://github.com/technehub-labs/dea-catalog-value-streams/blob/main/change-requests/CR-VS-09.md) is drafted ready-to-execute and will land as soon as these records exist.

items.title: Test gap: the customer workspace components (CustomerDetail / CustomerStatStrip / CustomerPipeline / NewCustomerPanel) have no component tests

labels.name: severity:low
labels.description: Test gaps, pure refactors, tech-debt, minor inconsistencies

items.body:
## What's untested

The lead's primary customer workspace is rendered entirely by components that have **zero component tests**:

- `components/customers/CustomerDetail.tsx` — the detail shell (info, locations, site measures, estimates).
- `components/customers/CustomerStatStrip.tsx` — the per-customer metric strip.
- `components/customers/CustomerPipeline.tsx` — the estimate-status funnel.
- `components/customers/NewCustomerPanel.tsx` — the create-customer form.

Only the pure helper `filterCustomers.ts` is tested (`__tests__/components/customers/filterCustomers.test.ts`). The E2E `customer-detail.spec.ts` covers page **load**, not component state, the stat/pipeline derivations, or the create form's submit/validation/error branches.

## Why it matters

- **CustomerPipeline already has a known correctness bug** (#162: it re-derives the estimate-status label inline instead of using `estimateStatusTone().label`, and the two disagree). A component test would have caught that divergence and would guard against it recurring.
- **NewCustomerPanel** is a write path (creates the root of the `Customer → Location → … → Invoice` chain). Its validation/error handling and submit wiring are completely unverified at the component level; the `customers/schema.ts` Zod schema is also untested per #124, so neither layer pins customer-create input rules.
- `CustomerStatStrip` derivations are customer-facing numbers with no test.

## Suggested coverage

- `CustomerPipeline.test.tsx` — assert the funnel counts/labels are derived via `estimateStatusTone()` (locking #162's fix).
- `CustomerStatStrip.test.tsx` — assert metric derivations for representative inputs.
- `NewCustomerPanel.test.tsx` — required-field validation, successful submit calls the create mutation, and the error path surfaces a message.
- `CustomerDetail.test.tsx` — renders the child sections from mocked data (smoke + empty-section states).

items.title: Structure implementation
items.body:
A solid architecture description like this becomes the backbone of a good engineering proposal, so I shaped it in clear, professional English while keeping it technically sharp and future‑proof.  

## 🚀 Microservice Architecture Description (Python 3.12, FastAPI, Django, Multi‑Tenancy CRM)

### **1. Overview**
The proposed solution is a **Python 3.12 microservice** designed to support a **multi‑tenant CRM platform for automobile insurance brokerages**. The service exposes a **FastAPI‑based API layer** for high‑performance, asynchronous operations, while **Django** is embedded as the internal application framework responsible for ORM, admin utilities, and CRUD scaffolding.  
This hybrid approach combines FastAPI’s speed and modern API design with Django’s mature ecosystem for data modeling and administrative workflows.

### **2. Multi‑Tenancy Model**
The system adopts a **schema‑based multi‑tenancy strategy** in PostgreSQL.  
Each brokerage (tenant) receives its own schema, isolating customer data, sales pipelines, insurance policies, and operational records.  
A **tenant resolver middleware** identifies the tenant from request metadata (e.g., subdomain, header, or token) and dynamically routes ORM operations to the correct schema.  
This ensures strong data isolation, simplified backups, and scalable onboarding of new brokerages.

### **3. Technology Stack**
- **Python 3.12**  
- **FastAPI** for the public API layer  
- **Django** for ORM, admin, and CRUD utilities  
- **PostgreSQL** as the primary relational database  
- **SQLAlchemy (optional)** for advanced query patterns  
- **Pydantic v2** for request/response validation  
- **Celery / Redis** for asynchronous background tasks (optional)  
- **Docker** for containerization  
- **OAuth2 / JWT** for authentication and tenant identification  

### **4. Service Responsibilities**
- Tenant onboarding and schema provisioning  
- CRUD operations for CRM entities (leads, customers, vehicles, policies, agents)  
- Workflow automation endpoints  
- Customizable dashboards and analytics  
- Audit logging and activity tracking  
- Integration endpoints for external insurance APIs  

### **5. Customizable Dashboards**
The microservice includes a **dashboard configuration engine** that allows each tenant to define:
- Custom widgets  
- Data sources (queries mapped to ORM models)  
- Layouts and visual components  
- Role‑based visibility rules  

The API exposes endpoints for:
- Widget registration  
- Dashboard layout management  
- Query execution with tenant‑scoped permissions  

The frontend (built by another team) will consume these endpoints to render dynamic dashboards.

### **6. Database Structure & Table Scripts**
The system provides **full SQL scripts** for provisioning:
- Global metadata tables (tenants, users, roles, permissions)  
- Per‑tenant schema tables (customers, leads, vehicles, quotes, policies, tasks, notes)  
- Dashboard configuration tables  
- Audit and logging tables  

Each table is generated through Django migrations, but raw SQL scripts are also included for environments requiring manual provisioning.

### **7. API Layer (FastAPI)**
FastAPI handles:
- Routing  
- Request validation  
- Authentication  
- Tenant resolution  
- Response serialization  

It communicates with Django’s ORM through a shared application context, ensuring consistent data access across both frameworks.

### **8. Deployment & Scalability**
The microservice is designed for:
- Horizontal scaling via container orchestration  
- Schema‑level isolation for performance tuning  
- Independent deployment from the frontend  
- CI/CD pipelines for automated migrations and tenant provisioning  

---

If you want, I can also generate **[[a full architecture diagram](guide://action?prefill=Tell%20me%20more%20about%3A%20a%20full%20architecture%20diagram)](guide://action?prefill=Tell%20me%20more%20about%3A%20a%20full%20architecture%20diagram)**, **[[a detailed list of database tables](guide://action?prefill=Tell%20me%20more%20about%3A%20a%20detailed%20list%20of%20database%20tables)](guide://action?prefill=Tell%20me%20more%20about%3A%20a%20detailed%20list%20of%20database%20tables)**, or **[[a complete technical specification document](guide://action?prefill=Tell%20me%20more%20about%3A%20a%20complete%20technical%20specification%20document)](guide://action?prefill=Tell%20me%20more%20about%3A%20a%20complete%20technical%20specification%20document)**.

items.title: RFC: Smart Schema Synthesizer
items.body:
## 1. Problem

Today, onboarding a source system into CDS is a manual, expert-driven exercise:

1. An admin hand-authors the org's [profile schema](https://github.com/wso2/identity-customer-data-service/blob/main/docs/concepts/profile-schema.md) — every attribute, its `value_type`, `mutability`, `merge_strategy`, `multi_valued` flag.
2. For every source system, someone works out which of that source's fields correspond to which CDS attribute, and writes the transformation by hand.
3. If three sources call the same real-world thing `email1`, `mail`, and `emailAddress`, all three mappings are authored separately and independently — and any mistake surfaces later as a duplicate profile or a failed unification rule.



**The core idea: customers should not have to configure mappings by hand. They should be able to keep the schemas they already have, hand CDS their data, and let CDS work out the rest.**

---

## 2. Goals / Non-goals

**Goals**

- Build a **per-source schema** from real data, without the customer describing their source up front.
- Build a **global CDS profile schema** — the canonical, org-wide profile shape — as the semantic union of all source schemas.
- Generate the **source → global transformation** for every source field, including name mapping, type coercion, and value normalisation.
- Recognise that semantically identical fields with different names (`email1`, `mail`, `emailAddress`) are the same attribute, using both field names *and* the values themselves.
- Keep a human in the loop: everything the synthesizer produces is a **proposal** that an admin reviews, edits, and approves before it goes live.


---

## 3. Concepts

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Source** | A registered system that sends data to CDS (a CRM, a loyalty app, a support desk). A **new first-class entity** (D2) — it carries its own endpoint, credentials, sample set, schema version, and mapping version. |
| **Source schema** | The inferred shape of *one* source's data, in that source's own vocabulary (`email1`, `fName`, `mobile_no`). |
| **Global profile schema** | The canonical org-wide CDS profile schema — the one the rest of CDS (unification, consent, merge) actually operates on. |
| **Mapping** | The per-source transformation: `source_field → global_attribute`, plus any type coercion / normalisation. |


The key structural point: **there are N + 1 schemas.** One per source, plus one global. The source schemas exist so the customer can keep speaking their own language, the global schema exists so CDS has one consistent internal vocabulary.

---

## 4. Intake modes

The customer can feed the synthesizer in three ways. All three converge on the same pipeline.

| Mode | How it works | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Push samples** | Register the sources in CDS, then POST a handful of representative payloads per source. | Fastest path. Good for evaluation and for sources that can't expose an endpoint. |
| **Bulk import** | Hand CDS a full export (CSV/JSON/NDJSON). Synthesis runs over the whole dataset, and the same import can then be replayed to actually load profiles. | Migration from an existing CDP/CRM. |

Sample size matters for inference quality — a single record can't tell you whether a field is nullable, multi-valued, or an enum. Suggested floor: **(How many, need AI team help) records per source**, with the UI warning below that and degrading confidence scores accordingly.

---

## 5. The synthesis pipeline

**1. Collect and stage.** Gather the sample set for every source in the job and hold it for the duration of the job only. 

**2. LLM synthesis call.** The model receives the samples from *all* sources together — cross-source context is what lets it see that `email1`, `mail`, and `emailAddress` are one concept plus the CDS schema contract (Which can be baked in): the legal `value_type` values, the three scopes, the `mutability` and `merge_strategy` options, the immutable core attributes it must never propose, and the IS-owned attributes it should map onto rather than recreate. It returns per-source schemas, a global schema, mappings, and a **confidence score with cited evidence** per cluster.

The model must justify every cluster against these signals, and the review UI renders them back to the admin:

| Signal | Example |
|---|---|
| Normalised name similarity | `email1`, `mail`, `emailAddress` → normalise to `email` |
| Value pattern | All three fields match the email regex at >95% |
| Value-set overlap | The same literal values (`jane@acme.com`) appear in all three fields |
| Statistical shape | Similar cardinality, length distribution, null rate |
| Type agreement | All three are single-valued strings |


**3. Global schema proposal.** Each cluster becomes one global attribute with:

- a canonical `attribute_name` including its scope prefix — `identity_attributes.email`, `traits.preferred_language`, `application_data.<app>.score`
- `value_type` — the narrowest type that covers all members
- `mutability` — defaults to `readWrite`; identifier-like attributes proposed as `writeOnce`
- `merge_strategy` — `overwrite` for single-valued, `combine` for multi-valued
- `display_name`, `multi_valued`, `canonical_values`, `sub_attributes` as inferred


**4. Review and approval.**

Nothing activates without an admin approving it.

| Band | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **High confidence** | Auto-accepted and collapsed. Visible and editable, but requires no action. Typical case: a cluster where names normalise identically *and* values match one format *and* value sets overlap. |
| **Low confidence** | Requires explicit per-item approval. Typical case: a cluster justified by name similarity alone, or a type the model had to widen to fit disagreeing sources. |
| **Unclustered** | Requires explicit per-item decision — accept into `application_data`, map onto an existing global attribute, or reject. |

**7. Activation.** The approved proposal is written as a new schema version and the mappings are attached to their sources.

---

## 6. Worked example

Three sources send a customer's email address:

```jsonc
// Source 1 — CRM
{ "email1": "Jane@ACME.com", "fName": "Jane", "mobile_no": "0771234567" }

// Source 2 — loyalty app
{ "mail": "jane@acme.com", "first_name": "Jane", "phone": "+94771234567" }

// Source 3 — support desk
{ "emailAddress": "jane@acme.com", "givenName": "Jane", "contactNumber": "94771234567" }
```

**Inferred source schemas** keep each source's own names — `email1`, `mail`, `emailAddress` stay as-is in their respective source profiles.

**Clustering** finds all three carry email-shaped values, overlapping value sets, and names that normalise to `email`. Same for the name fields and the phone fields.

**Global schema:**

| Attribute | Type | Multi-valued | Merge |
|---|---|---|---|
| `identity_attributes.email` | `string` | no | `overwrite` |
| `identity_attributes.given_name` | `string` | no | `overwrite` |
| `identity_attributes.phone_number` | `string` | no | `overwrite` |

**Mappings:**

| Source | Source field | Global attribute | Transformation |
|---|---|---|---|
| CRM | `email1` | `identity_attributes.email` | lowercase |
| Loyalty | `mail` | `identity_attributes.email` | — |
| Support | `emailAddress` | `identity_attributes.email` | — |
| CRM | `mobile_no` | `identity_attributes.phone_number` | local → E.164 (`+94`) |
| Loyalty | `phone` | `identity_attributes.phone_number` | — |
| Support | `contactNumber` | `identity_attributes.phone_number` | prefix `+` |


## 8. Lifecycle after activation (Maybe stuff)

Sources change. The synthesizer needs an answer for what happens on day 200, not just day 1.

- **Drift detection.** When ingest sees a field that isn't in the source's schema, or a value that violates the inferred type/format, record it rather than silently dropping it.
- **Re-synthesis.** An admin can re-run synthesis on a source against recent live traffic. The output is a *diff* against the active schema, reviewed the same way.
- **Versioning.** Both the global schema and each source mapping are versioned, with the active version recorded per source. Rollback is a version pointer change.
- **Additive-only by default.** New attributes and new mappings can be auto-proposed; anything that changes or removes an existing attribute requires explicit approval, because profiles already hold data under that definition.

+# The shop as a bundle: publish it, run it, look at it, take it down
+
+The same little shop as `examples/shop` (200 customers, 30 products, 200 000 generated order lines, one layer per catalog), but
+as a **bundle of twelve SQL pipelines** instead of a dbt project. It needs no dbt, no extra image and no terminal on the cluster:
+only the `stardelt` command line, signed in.
+
+| Layer | Catalog | Pipelines | What |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| schemas | `bronze`, `silver`, `gold` | `shop-01-bronze`, `shop-02-silver`, `shop-03-gold` | one schema in each catalog |
+| bronze | `bronze` | `shop-04-customers`, `shop-05-products`, `shop-06-lines` | the two small seed tables and the generated order lines |
+| silver | `silver` | `shop-07-stg-cust`, `shop-08-stg-prod`, `shop-09-stg-lines` | three views with clean names and types |
+| gold | `gold` | `shop-10-revenue`, `shop-11-ltv`, `shop-12-mix` | `daily_revenue`, `customer_ltv` (window functions), `product_mix` |
+
+A pipeline runs exactly one statement, so every step of the shop is one pipeline; they run in name order, and the number in the
+name is that order. Nothing is downloaded and nothing large is stored in Git: the order lines are built inside the query engine
+from the line number (`scale` of them, a multiple of 1000, default 200 000).
+
+## Before you start (an administrator, once)
+
+- The catalogs `bronze`, `silver` and `gold` exist, and the group named in `bundle.yaml` (`ownerGroup: demo`) has a pipeline
+  principal (`pipeline-demo`) that may write to them. In the platform repository: `make demo-access GROUP=demo`. For another
+  group, change `ownerGroup` and `runAs` in `bundle.yaml`.
+- You are a member of that group and have signed in: `stardelt login`.
+
+## The loop
+
+```bash
+cd examples/shop-bundle
+stardelt bundle validate .            # offline: twelve pipelines for each of the two targets
+stardelt bundle plan . -t dev         # twelve lines "would-create"
+stardelt bundle deploy . -t dev       # twelve pipelines, named dev-<your name>-shop-NN-..., no schedule
+stardelt bundle run . -t dev          # starts them one after the other, waits for each, stops at the first that fails
+stardelt bundle summary . -t dev      # what runs on the stage, from which commit
+```
+
+Then look at the results in the **SQL editor** (the tables of the `dev` target live in the schema `shop_dev`):
+
+```sql
+select * from gold.shop_dev.daily_revenue order by order_date desc limit 7;
+select * from gold.shop_dev.customer_ltv order by value_rank limit 10;
+select * from gold.shop_dev.product_mix order by revenue desc limit 10;
+```
+
+Every statement of the run is in your **Query log** with the source "Pipeline task". The **Deployments** page shows the bundle, the
+target, the commit and who deployed it.
+
+Change something (for example the `scale` variable in `bundle.yaml`), then:
+
+```bash
+stardelt bundle plan . -t dev --diff  # shows what would change in each pipeline
+stardelt bundle deploy . -t dev
+stardelt bundle run . -t dev --only shop-06-lines
+```
+
+`--only` takes the name with or without the `dev-<your name>-` prefix. After `scale` changed, run the pipelines from `shop-06-lines`
+on again (the tables downstream are rebuilt from the lines).
+
+## The two targets
+
+- `dev` (mode `development`): your own copy, pipelines named `dev-<your name>-shop-NN-...`, no schedule, tables in the schema
+  `shop_dev`. Pipeline names of a development copy are limited to 40 characters, so a sign-in name of up to 18 characters fits.
+- `prod` (mode `production`, `runAs: pipeline-demo`): the shared copy an administrator publishes once, pipelines named
+  `shop-NN-...`, tables in the schema `shop`. It has no schedule either; run it with `stardelt bundle run . -t prod`.
+
+## Take it down
+
+`stardelt bundle destroy . -t dev --yes` removes the pipelines. The tables stay (a pipeline cannot be told to drop what it made);
+drop them in the SQL editor, one statement at a time:
+
+```sql
+drop view silver.shop_dev.stg_order_lines;
+drop view silver.shop_dev.stg_products;
+drop view silver.shop_dev.stg_customers;
+drop table gold.shop_dev.product_mix;
+drop table gold.shop_dev.customer_ltv;
+drop table gold.shop_dev.daily_revenue;
+drop table bronze.shop_dev.order_lines;
+drop table bronze.shop_dev.products;
+drop table bronze.shop_dev.customers;
+drop schema gold.shop_dev;
+drop schema silver.shop_dev;
+drop schema bronze.shop_dev;
+```
+
+## How it differs from the dbt version
+
+- No tests (dbt's twenty tests have no counterpart in a plain pipeline), and `daily_revenue` is rebuilt on every run instead of
+  merging the last three days.
+- Seeds are `values` lists inside two statements (`sql/04_customers.sql`, `sql/05_products.sql`), generated from the CSV files of
+  `examples/shop/seeds`.
+- The statements were checked for syntax only (parsed with the Trino dialect) and the bundle with `stardelt bundle validate`.
+  Nobody has run this example, or the dbt version, against a live cluster yet: the first run is the check (demos#31, slice A),
+  and a failure is a bug in this example, file it. Times and memory are recorded here after that run, never guessed.

diff --git a/examples/shop-bundle/sql/06_order_lines.sql b/examples/shop-bundle/sql/06_order_lines.sql
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..688a0e6
--- /dev/null
+++ b/examples/shop-bundle/sql/06_order_lines.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,21 @@
+-- The compute of the example: ${params.scale} order lines built inside the query engine, nothing downloaded and
+-- nothing stored in Git. `sequence` is limited to 10 000 entries, so the numbers come from two small sequences
+-- (blocks of 1000 times 1000); ${params.scale} must be a multiple of 1000. Customer, product, quantity and day come
+-- from a hash of the line number: the same lines every run.
+create or replace table bronze.${params.schema}.order_lines as
+with blocks as (
+    select x from unnest(sequence(0, ${params.scale} / 1000 - 1)) as t(x)
+),
+within_block as (
+    select y from unnest(sequence(1, 1000)) as t(y)
+),
+numbered as (
+    select x * 1000 + y as order_line_id from blocks cross join within_block
+)
+select
+    order_line_id,
+    1 + mod(mod(from_big_endian_64(xxhash64(to_utf8('c' || cast(order_line_id as varchar)))), 200) + 200, 200) as customer_id,
+    1 + mod(mod(from_big_endian_64(xxhash64(to_utf8('p' || cast(order_line_id as varchar)))), 30) + 30, 30) as product_id,
+    1 + mod(mod(from_big_endian_64(xxhash64(to_utf8('q' || cast(order_line_id as varchar)))), 5) + 5, 5) as quantity,
+    date_add('day', mod(mod(from_big_endian_64(xxhash64(to_utf8('d' || cast(order_line_id as varchar)))), 365) + 365, 365), date '2025-01-01') as order_date
+from numbered

+-- Rebuilt on every run (the dbt version of the shop merges the last three days instead).
+create or replace table gold.${params.schema}.daily_revenue as
+select
+    l.order_date,
+    count(*) as order_lines,
+    sum(l.quantity) as units,
+    sum(l.quantity * p.unit_price) as revenue
+from silver.${params.schema}.stg_order_lines l
+join silver.${params.schema}.stg_products p on p.product_id = l.product_id
+group by l.order_date
diff --git a/examples/shop-bundle/sql/11_customer_ltv.sql b/examples/shop-bundle/sql/11_customer_ltv.sql
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..c3a1ec1
--- /dev/null
+++ b/examples/shop-bundle/sql/11_customer_ltv.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,27 @@
+-- Window functions: each customer's lifetime value, their rank, and the share of revenue the best customers make up.
+create or replace table gold.${params.schema}.customer_ltv as
+with per_customer as (
+    select
+        l.customer_id,
+        count(*) as order_lines,
+        sum(l.quantity * p.unit_price) as lifetime_value,
+        min(l.order_date) as first_order,
+        max(l.order_date) as last_order
+    from silver.${params.schema}.stg_order_lines l
+    join silver.${params.schema}.stg_products p on p.product_id = l.product_id
+    group by l.customer_id
+)
+select
+    c.customer_id,
+    c.customer_name,
+    c.country,
+    c.segment,
+    pc.order_lines,
+    pc.lifetime_value,
+    pc.first_order,
+    pc.last_order,
+    rank() over (order by pc.lifetime_value desc) as value_rank,
+    sum(pc.lifetime_value) over (order by pc.lifetime_value desc rows between unbounded preceding and current row)
+        / sum(pc.lifetime_value) over () as cumulative_share
+from silver.${params.schema}.stg_customers c
+join per_customer pc on pc.customer_id = c.customer_id
diff --git a/examples/shop-bundle/sql/12_product_mix.sql b/examples/shop-bundle/sql/12_product_mix.sql

@@ -0,0 +1,12 @@
+create or replace table gold.${params.schema}.product_mix as
+select
+    p.product_id,
+    p.product_name,
+    p.category,
+    sum(l.quantity) as units,
+    sum(l.quantity * p.unit_price) as revenue,
+    sum(l.quantity * p.unit_price) / sum(sum(l.quantity * p.unit_price)) over () as revenue_share,
+    rank() over (partition by p.category order by sum(l.quantity * p.unit_price) desc) as rank_in_category
+from silver.${params.schema}.stg_order_lines l
+join silver.${params.schema}.stg_products p on p.product_id = l.product_id
+group by p.product_id, p.product_name, p.category

+
+import csv
+import pathlib
+import re
+
+import yaml
+
+EXAMPLES = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "examples"
+BUNDLE = EXAMPLES / "shop-bundle"
+DBT = EXAMPLES / "shop"
+
+# The limits of a pipeline statement (Nova: one statement, at most 20 000 characters) and of a development name.
+MAX_STATEMENT = 20_000
+MAX_NAME = 17  # "dev-" + a sign-in name of up to 18 characters + "-" + the name stays within 40 characters
+
+PARAM = re.compile(r"\$\{params\.([a-z][a-z0-9_]*)\}")
+VAR = re.compile(r"\$\{var\.([A-Za-z0-9_]+)\}")
+
+
+def pipelines():
+    return [
+        (path, yaml.safe_load(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
+        for path in sorted((BUNDLE / "resources").glob("*.yaml"))
+    ]
+
+
+def manifest():
+    return yaml.safe_load((BUNDLE / "bundle.yaml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
+
+
+def test_every_pipeline_names_a_statement_file_that_exists():
+    found = pipelines()
+    assert len(found) == 12
+    for path, doc in found:
+        statement = BUNDLE / doc["sqlFile"]
+        assert statement.is_file(), f"{path.name}: {doc['sqlFile']} is missing"
+        assert statement.stem == path.stem, f"{path.name} and {statement.name} do not belong together"
+    on_disk = sorted(p.name for p in (BUNDLE / "sql").glob("*.sql"))
+    assert on_disk == sorted(f"{path.stem}.sql" for path, _ in found), "a statement file belongs to no pipeline"
+
+
+def test_names_are_short_unique_and_run_in_file_order():
+    names = [doc["name"] for _, doc in pipelines()]
+    assert len(set(names)) == len(names)
+    for (path, _), name in zip(pipelines(), names):
+        assert re.fullmatch(r"shop-\d\d-[a-z-]+", name), name
+        assert len(name) <= MAX_NAME, f"{name} is {len(name)} characters"
+        assert name.split("-")[1] == path.stem.split("_")[0], f"{name} does not carry the number of {path.name}"
+    assert names == sorted(names), "bundle run starts the pipelines in name order: the order of the files must be the same"
+
+
+def test_a_statement_uses_only_the_params_its_pipeline_sets():
+    for _, doc in pipelines():
+        sql = (BUNDLE / doc["sqlFile"]).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+        used = set(PARAM.findall(sql))
+        assert used <= set(doc.get("params", {})), f"{doc['name']} uses {used - set(doc.get('params', {}))} without setting it"
+        assert set(doc.get("params", {})) <= used, f"{doc['name']} sets a param its statement never uses"
+
+
+def test_a_statement_is_one_statement_within_the_limit():
+    for _, doc in pipelines():
+        sql = (BUNDLE / doc["sqlFile"]).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+        code = "\n".join(line for line in sql.splitlines() if not line.strip().startswith("--")).strip().rstrip(";")
+        assert ";" not in code, f"{doc['name']} holds more than one statement"
+        assert 0 < len(sql) <= MAX_STATEMENT, f"{doc['name']}: {len(sql)} characters"
+        assert "\0" not in sql
+
+
+def test_the_manifest_declares_every_variable_and_every_target_sets_it():
+    declared = manifest()["variables"]
+    used = set()
+    for path, _ in pipelines():
+        used |= set(VAR.findall(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
+    assert used == set(declared), f"used {sorted(used)}, declared {sorted(declared)}"
+    for name, target in manifest()["targets"].items():
+        assert set(target["variables"]) == set(declared), name
+    assert manifest()["targets"]["dev"]["variables"]["schema"] != manifest()["targets"]["prod"]["variables"]["schema"]
+    assert manifest()["targets"]["prod"]["runAs"] == "pipeline-" + manifest()["bundle"]["ownerGroup"]
+
+
+def test_the_seed_statements_hold_exactly_the_rows_of_the_dbt_seeds():
+    for table, seed in (("04_customers", "customers"), ("05_products", "products")):
+        with open(DBT / "seeds" / f"{seed}.csv", newline="") as handle:
+            rows = list(csv.DictReader(handle))
+        sql = (BUNDLE / "sql" / f"{table}.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+        values = [line for line in sql.splitlines() if line.startswith("    (")]
+        assert len(values) == len(rows), f"{table}: {len(values)} rows, the seed has {len(rows)}"
+        first, last = rows[0], rows[-1]
+        assert f"({first['id']}, '{first['name']}'" in values[0]
+        assert f"({last['id']}, '{last['name']}'" in values[-1]
+
+
+def test_the_generated_lines_use_the_same_hashes_as_the_dbt_model():
+    def hashes(text):
+        return sorted(line.strip() for line in text.splitlines() if "xxhash64" in line)
+
+    model = (DBT / "models" / "bronze" / "order_lines.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+    statement = (BUNDLE / "sql" / "06_order_lines.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+    assert len(hashes(statement)) == 4
+    assert hashes(statement) == hashes(model)
+
+
+def test_the_layers_are_the_catalogs_of_the_dbt_example():
+    targets = {
+        "04_customers": "bronze", "05_products": "bronze", "06_order_lines": "bronze",
+        "07_stg_customers": "silver", "08_stg_products": "silver", "09_stg_order_lines": "silver",
+        "10_daily_revenue": "gold", "11_customer_ltv": "gold", "12_product_mix": "gold",
+    }
+    for stem, catalog in targets.items():
+        sql = (BUNDLE / "sql" / f"{stem}.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+        assert re.search(rf"create or replace (table|view) {catalog}\.\$\{{params\.schema\}}\.", sql), stem
```

items.title: Patient migration

milestone.title: Later
milestone.description: Unscheduled. Pulled into an R milestone when a customer or a regulation needs it. Holds the open remainder of M0-M2, M6-M9 and MVP 1 (MVP 1 items keep the release:MVP 1 label).

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

No hospital arrives empty. A customer switching to this platform brings 200,000 to 2 million existing patient records from a legacy HMS, and frequently from more than one: an old registration system, a separate laboratory system, a pharmacy package and a pile of scanned case sheets. There is currently no capability to bring any of it in.

The consequence of that absence is that go-live becomes a hard reset. A patient who has attended the hospital for eleven years arrives at the registration desk on day one and is a new patient with a new UHID. The ward nurse cannot see the previous admission, the consultant cannot see last month's creatinine trend, the pharmacist cannot see the documented penicillin allergy, and the billing desk cannot see the outstanding balance. That is not an inconvenience; it is a clinical safety problem and the single most common reason a hospital refuses to switch systems.

Patient migration is also the highest-risk operation in the entire onboarding programme, because it is where identity errors become permanent. Merging two different patients into one record because they share a name and an approximate age puts one person's allergies and results into another person's chart. The MDM rule that patient identity matching must be deterministic and probabilistic exists precisely because bad matching corrupts everything downstream.

The regulatory frame is dense. Under the **DPDP Act 2023** this is bulk processing of sensitive personal data by the platform as Data Processor on the customer's instruction; it requires a lawful basis, purpose limitation, and the ability to honour access, correction and erasure requests over migrated data exactly as over native data. **ABDM** means migrated patients may hold an ABHA that must be linked rather than duplicated, and that migrated records only flow to a Health Information User under a valid consent artefact. **FHIR R4** is the canonical clinical shape, so legacy structures must be mapped to `Patient`, `Encounter`, `Observation`, `Condition`, `MedicationRequest` and `DiagnosticReport` at the boundary. **NABH** requires retrievable prior records. Data residency means migration staging must sit inside the customer's country region and never in a shared or non-prod environment.

Affected roles: the implementation lead and data-migration engineer running the load, the hospital admin who signs off the reconciliation, the medical records officer who owns record integrity, the ward nurse and consultant who depend on prior history being present and correct, and the DPO, who must be able to evidence the lawful basis and the retention position for every migrated record.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As an** implementation lead migrating a customer from a legacy hospital system
**I want** to load, map, match, validate and commit their historical patient master and clinical history into the platform through a staged, reversible and fully reconciled pipeline
**So that** on go-live every returning patient is recognised with their correct identifier, history and balances, and no two patients have been merged into one.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A migration pipeline with explicit stages — `landed → profiled → mapped → matched → validated → committed` — where each stage produces an artefact the customer signs off before the next begins, and nothing reaches the live clinical store before commit.
* Ingestion of delimited extracts and database dumps into a per-customer staging schema inside the customer's residency region, encrypted, access-restricted and retention-capped.
* Source profiling: per-column completeness, cardinality, format anomalies and free-text density, so the customer sees the real state of their data before committing to a mapping.
* Field mapping from legacy shapes to the canonical FHIR R4 resources, with a saved, versioned mapping per customer and per source system, plus code-system mapping for sex, marital status, blood group, legacy diagnosis codes to ICD, and legacy test codes to the test master.
* Patient identity resolution: deterministic keys first (ABHA number, legacy UHID within the same source, mobile plus date of birth), probabilistic scoring second, an explicit human review band, and a recorded match decision with score and decider for every non-trivial case.
* Legacy identifier retention: every migrated patient keeps its source-system identifier as a searchable secondary identifier so front-desk staff can find a patient by the number printed on their old card.
* Clinical history migration scoped to what is safe and useful: encounters, diagnoses, allergies and adverse reactions, medications, laboratory results with units and reference ranges, and document attachments — with anything unmappable quarantined rather than guessed.
* Financial carry-forward of outstanding patient balances and open insurance or TPA claims as opening entries, not reconstructed transaction history.
* Reconciliation reporting: counts by entity in and out, rejected and quarantined rows with reasons, and a signed reconciliation certificate that #623 requires.
* A tested rollback for the commit stage, and a documented cutover procedure including the delta load for records created in the legacy system between the main load and go-live.

**Out of scope**

* Staff and practitioner records — owned by *Staff import* (#617); migrated encounters reference practitioners that import created.
* Medicine and laboratory catalogues that migrated prescriptions and results resolve against — owned by #619 and #620, both of which must land first.
* Departments and facilities the migrated records attach to — owned by #615 and #616.
* Opening stock, batches and expiry — owned by SupplyConnect and PharmaConnect inventory onboarding.
* OCR digitisation of scanned paper case sheets into structured clinical data; scanned documents migrate as attachments only.
* ABHA creation for patients who do not hold one; existing ABHA numbers are linked, new ones are not minted during migration.
* Ongoing bidirectional synchronisation with the legacy system after cutover.

---

## Recommended Solution

Build migration as a Temporal-orchestrated pipeline driven by a `migration` module in the Go 1.26 modular monolith, with all staging inside the customer's regional PostgreSQL 16 cluster. The hard rule is separation: staging lives in a dedicated schema (`mig_<tenant_slug>`) that the live clinical data-access layer cannot read, and promotion into the live store happens only through the same tenant-scoped, RLS-enforced write path that native records use. Migration does not get a privileged back door into the clinical tables — it uses the domain services, so every invariant, every audit record and every event is produced exactly as for a record created at the front desk.

### Data model

```sql
CREATE TABLE migration_run (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, facility_id uuid,
  source_system text NOT NULL,          -- customer's legacy product name + version
  run_kind text NOT NULL,               -- full | delta
  stage text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'landed',
  mapping_version int NOT NULL,
  signed_off_by text, signed_off_at timestamptz,
  started_at timestamptz, committed_at timestamptz,
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, source_system, run_kind, started_at)
);

CREATE TABLE migration_patient_stage (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES migration_run(id),
  source_row_ref text NOT NULL,         -- legacy primary key, kept for reconciliation
  legacy_uhid text,
  abha_number_token text,               -- tokenised; raw ABHA/Aadhaar never stored
  name_given text, name_family text, dob date, sex text, mobile text,
  address jsonb,
  fhir_patient jsonb,                   -- mapped FHIR R4 Patient resource
  match_decision text,                  -- new | linked | review | rejected
  matched_patient_id uuid, match_score numeric, match_rule text,
  decided_by text, decided_at timestamptz,
  validation_state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  errors jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]'::jsonb,
  committed_patient_id uuid,
  UNIQUE (run_id, source_row_ref)
);

CREATE TABLE migration_clinical_stage (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id uuid NOT NULL, patient_stage_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES migration_patient_stage(id),
  resource_type text NOT NULL,          -- Encounter | Condition | AllergyIntolerance |
                                        -- MedicationRequest | Observation | DiagnosticReport
  source_row_ref text NOT NULL,
  fhir_resource jsonb NOT NULL,
  validation_state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  quarantine_reason text,
  committed_resource_id uuid,
  UNIQUE (run_id, resource_type, source_row_ref)
);

CREATE TABLE migration_reconciliation (
  run_id uuid NOT NULL, entity text NOT NULL,
  source_count bigint NOT NULL, staged_count bigint NOT NULL,
  committed_count bigint NOT NULL, quarantined_count bigint NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (run_id, entity)
);
```

Aadhaar numbers are never stored, in line with the India profile; where a legacy system holds them, the mapper drops the column at ingestion and records that it did so. ABHA numbers are tokenised at rest.

### Identity resolution

The matcher runs in two passes, and its output is a decision with a recorded rule, never an implicit side effect.

* Deterministic: ABHA token exact; `(source_system, legacy_uhid)` exact for re-runs and deltas; `(mobile, dob)` exact where both are populated and the mobile is not shared by more than a configured number of records — shared family mobiles are common and are explicitly excluded from auto-linking above that threshold.
* Probabilistic: Jaro-Winkler on normalised names combined with date-of-birth proximity, sex agreement, address pincode agreement and mobile partial agreement, producing a score.
* Bands are configuration: above `auto_link_threshold` link automatically; between the thresholds set `review` and require a human decision in the console; below `auto_new_threshold` create a new patient. **The review band never auto-resolves.** A run cannot progress from `matched` to `validated` while any row sits in `review`.

Every merge is reversible: `committed_patient_id` plus `match_rule` and `match_score` are retained, so an incorrect link found after go-live can be unmerged with a full record of what was joined and by whom.

### Orchestration and API surface

`PatientMigrationWorkflow` (Temporal) runs stage activities with checkpoints, and the commit stage fans out in bounded batches through the clinical domain services. Commit is idempotent on `(run_id, source_row_ref)`, so a resumed commit after an interruption never double-creates.

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations` | Open a run; returns staging upload credentials |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:profile` | Produce the source profile report |
| PUT | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}/mapping` | Save a mapping version |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:match` | Run identity resolution |
| GET | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}/review-queue` | Rows in the review band |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}/review/{rowId}:decide` | `link` \| `new` \| `reject` + reason |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:validate` | Full validation, no writes |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:commit` | Reviewer-only; `Idempotency-Key` required |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:rollback` | Within the rollback window |
| GET | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}/reconciliation` | Signed reconciliation certificate |

### Events

Commit emits the platform's ordinary domain events with a `migrated: true` attribute so downstream consumers can distinguish historical load from live activity and suppress notifications: `PatientRegistered`, `EncounterRecorded`, `LabResultReady`, `PrescriptionIssued`. Migration-specific events on `platform.migration.*`: `MigrationStageCompleted`, `MigrationCommitted`, `MigrationRolledBack`.

```json
{ "event": "MigrationCommitted", "run_id": "…", "tenant_id": "…",
  "source_system": "LegacyHMS 7.4", "run_kind": "full",
  "patients_committed": 486213, "patients_linked": 11904,
  "resources_committed": 9127440, "quarantined": 2183, "version": 1 }
```

Suppression matters: without the `migrated` flag, committing 480,000 patients would emit hundreds of thousands of WhatsApp notifications.

### Authorisation

```
type migration_run
  relations
    define organisation: [organisation]
    define migration_engineer: [user]
    define reviewer: reviewer from organisation
    define customer_signatory: [user]
    define can_stage: migration_engineer
    define can_decide_match: migration_engineer or customer_signatory
    define can_commit: reviewer and customer_signatory
    define can_rollback: reviewer
```

`can_commit` requires both a platform reviewer and a customer signatory: the customer must own the decision to load their own patient data. Staging tables hold sensitive personal data and are excluded from analytics, from backups outside the region and from non-prod entirely — non-prod uses synthetic data only, without exception.

### Sequencing and risks

Depends on #615, #616, #617, and on #619 and #620 landing first because migrated prescriptions and results must resolve against a populated drug and test master. Blocks #623, which requires a signed reconciliation certificate. Principal risks: incorrect patient merges — mitigated by the never-auto-resolving review band, retained match evidence and a supported unmerge; unmappable clinical data being silently dropped — mitigated by quarantine-with-reason and a reconciliation certificate whose counts must balance before sign-off; and delta drift between the main load and cutover — mitigated by a documented delta run keyed on legacy modification timestamps and a freeze window agreed in the cutover plan.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a customer with live facilities, active departments, imported staff and populated medicine and laboratory catalogues
**When** the migration engineer lands a 486,000-patient extract, profiles it, saves a mapping to FHIR R4, runs matching that auto-links 11,904 patients on ABHA token and legacy UHID and refers 3,140 to review, the customer signatory clears the review queue, validation passes, and reviewer plus signatory jointly call `:commit`
**Then** every staged patient is created through the clinical domain services with its legacy UHID retained as a searchable secondary identifier, clinical resources are attached, domain events carry `migrated: true` so no patient notification is sent, and the reconciliation certificate shows source, staged and committed counts balancing to zero variance across all entities.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a migration run where 3,140 rows sit in the probabilistic review band and 41 have not been decided
**When** a reviewer attempts `:commit`
**Then** the request is rejected with `409 UNRESOLVED_MATCHES` and the count of undecided rows, no patient is created, no event is published, the run remains at `matched`, and the console deep-links to the outstanding review queue. The same rejection occurs if the customer signatory approval is absent, even when every match is decided.

### Edge Cases

* Two legacy records share a mobile number and surname because they are mother and daughter — the shared-mobile threshold excludes the pair from deterministic auto-linking and both are referred to review; a wrong merge here would attach a child's records to an adult chart.
* A legacy patient already exists in the platform because they were registered during the parallel-run period — the delta run links to the existing patient and does not create a duplicate.
* A laboratory result carries a legacy test code with no mapping in the test master — the resource is quarantined with `unmapped_test_code` and named in the reconciliation report; it is not committed with a guessed code or a null.
* An observation arrives with a value but no unit of measure — quarantined; a creatinine result without units is clinically unsafe to display.
* A migrated allergy record is free text only — committed as an `AllergyIntolerance` with a text-only code and flagged for clinical review, rather than being force-mapped to a coded substance.
* `:commit` is interrupted at 60% by a node restart — the workflow resumes from its checkpoint, the `(run_id, source_row_ref)` uniqueness prevents re-creation, and the final counts match a clean run.
* An incorrect auto-link is discovered two weeks after go-live — the retained match evidence supports an unmerge that separates the records and preserves the audit trail of both the original link and its reversal.
* A migration engineer scoped to customer A queries customer B's staging schema — refused by row-level security and the tenant-scoped data-access layer, and logged as a tenant-boundary violation.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** returning patients are recognised at the registration desk on go-live morning with their old card number, their history, their allergies and their outstanding balance intact.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** customers can switch systems without losing their clinical record estate, removing the principal commercial objection to migration and avoiding a parallel-run period longer than the agreed cutover window.
* **Success metric or validation method:** reconciliation variance of zero across patients, encounters, observations and documents between source, staged and committed counts, signed by the customer before go-live; quarantine rate below 0.5% of clinical resources, each with a named reason; incorrect-merge rate of zero in a stratified manual audit of 500 auto-linked records per customer; commit throughput sufficient to load 500,000 patients and 9 million clinical resources inside an 8-hour cutover window.
* **Monitoring period:** through cutover and 30 days after go-live, tracking `migration_quarantine_total` by reason, `migration_commit_rows_per_second`, patient unmerge requests raised by the medical records officer, and front-desk duplicate-registration rate compared against the pre-migration baseline.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

**Guardrail:** Automated Testing — "Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework", at production data volumes.
**Reason:** The critical journey for this story includes committing hundreds of thousands of patients and millions of clinical resources. That volume cannot be exercised inside a per-pull-request CI budget, and it cannot be exercised against customer data at all, because PHI never appears in non-prod.
**Alternative validation:** Playwright covers the full console journey — land, profile, map, match, review, validate, commit, reconcile and roll back — against a 500-patient synthetic fixture in CI. Full-volume behaviour is validated by a scheduled weekly load run in a pre-production environment in the same residency region, using a 500,000-patient synthetic dataset generated to match the profile of real customer extracts, asserting commit throughput, reconciliation variance of zero and a successful rollback.
**Residual risk:** A throughput or memory regression that only manifests above the synthetic fixture size is detected at the weekly load run rather than at the pull request that introduced it, giving up to seven days of exposure. This is accepted because no customer commit runs without a preceding dry-run and reconciliation, so a regression is caught before it affects live data.
**Approved by:** Implementation lead and platform engineering lead, recorded on the story.

All other guardrails apply in full. The match-review queue is a user-facing Next.js 16 surface under the accessibility guardrail, and the observability guardrail is applied strictly: migration logs reference staging row identifiers and error codes only, never patient names, identifiers or clinical values.

items.title: Add optional PDF and image inputs to extract.ai

type.name: Enhancement
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Outcome

Allow ordinary `extract.ai` calls and YAML recipes to extract structured information directly from PDFs and images, optionally combined with text. This should make diagrams, photographs, scanned text, and document layout available to a capable model without requiring callers to convert everything to Markdown first.

The current Responses adapter in `wrangles/openai_responses.py` constructs a text-only user message from `format_input_data(data)`. Selecting a vision-capable model alone therefore does not supply the original document or image.

## Goals and acceptance criteria

- **Explicit attachment inputs.** Define a small, clear public contract for one or more PDF/image attachments per input record, with optional text context. Support PDF-only, image-only, and mixed requests. Local files are an initial use case; agree on the other supported forms, such as bytes, URLs, or provider file IDs, during design. Ordinary text containing a path or URL must not silently trigger loading or uploading.
- **Preserve compatibility.** Keep existing text-only behavior, structured-output schemas, saved models, configuration precedence, and return shapes. A Python input list currently represents separate extractions; do not reinterpret that list as attachments to one extraction. Recipe input-column selection, row association, and output order must remain predictable.
- **Use the existing wrangle.** Expose this through the Python API and normal YAML `extract.ai` configuration. Recipes continue to control discovery, mapping, checkpoints, and subsequent stages. Callers should not need a parallel custom API client.
- **Send actual multimodal content.** Start with the OpenAI Responses path and caller-selected supported models. Validate missing files, unsupported formats, size limits, and incompatible model/provider/protocol combinations with actionable errors. Never silently discard visual inputs. Document any upload lifecycle introduced. Hosted PDF/image input should not require Docling or a local GPU.
- **Retain operational behavior.** Integrate with existing credential resolution, including model/group-scoped credentials, retries, concurrency, request storage, metadata, and logging. Cache identity must include attachment content and relevant request settings: replacing a file at the same path must invalidate the result. Distinguish attachment ordering and association with records.
- **Account for usage.** Preserve provider-reported input/output tokens and available cached-input, cache-write, and reasoning breakdowns, along with model identity, request status, timing, and request/response identifiers. Include failed or incomplete attempts when usage is returned. Do not double-count reasoning already included in output tokens; missing usage is unknown, not zero. Diagnostics should distinguish local cache reuse from a new model call and enable downstream cost estimates without hard-coding price tables into the wrangle. Normal logs must not expose credentials or full binary/Base64 payloads.
- **Enable source references.** Preserve stable file/image identifiers and make them usable in caller-defined output schemas and prompts requesting page numbers, quotes, or image references. These remain model-produced claims requiring validation. This first slice does not promise accurate bounding boxes or table-cell coordinates. Native PDF/Docling location matching, known crop coordinates, and highlight generation can be added downstream.

## Verification and documentation

- Add small synthetic or sanitized fixtures and focused tests covering text-only regressions, PDF/image request construction, mixed and multiple attachments, row/list semantics, source association, validation failures, attachment cache identity, credential isolation, and incomplete-response usage.
- Provide simple Python and YAML recipe examples, including text plus an attachment and multiple input records. Document the supported models/protocols, input forms, limits, and diagnostics.
- Report offline tests separately from live-service validation. Validate the supported paths with an in-scope PDF trial, a standalone image, and mixed text/image input; retain actual per-attempt usage and timings.
- Use the RSGroup SF_AMF60 case as a downstream integration check. Review remaining quality gaps explicitly; the first usable slice may have documented extraction errors.

## Evidence motivating this work

A local RSGroup experiment supplied the original SF_AMF60 PDF to Astra at medium reasoning, then performed a separate mapping call. Against 30 frozen source checks, the PDF workflow achieved **27 pass, 2 partial, 1 absent**, compared with **15 pass, 7 partial, 8 absent** for the existing Docling/Granite-to-text workflow using Luna. Both found four product variants.

The successful PDF discovery and mapping calls used **54,056 input and 30,133 output tokens**, estimated at **$2.18** using the experiment's September 10, 2026 rates. Including an initial incomplete attempt, the experiment cost approximately **$3.62**. Model, prompt, workflow, and output budget differed, so this is encouraging evidence rather than a controlled modality-only comparison.

Local, currently uncommitted RSGroup references: `run_pdf_vision.py`, `functions_pdf_vision.py`, `recipes/pdf_vision.recipe`, and `pipeline/extraction/pdf_vision_api.py`. The local report and accounting are under `.data/pdf-vision/SF_AMF60/091026.02/`. Treat this prototype as design evidence, not the required public API.

## Scope and handoff

This issue concerns reusable WranglesPY inputs. Product discovery schemas, customer attribute mapping and overrides, complete per-product rows, mapping-validation fixes, Excel presentation, and Docling provenance resolution remain RSGroup responsibilities. Deployment and Excel UI exposure require separate follow-up where needed.

Eric will start a WranglesPY task from this issue. Resume RSGroup integration once the capability is available.

Related diagnostics work: [#1172](https://github.com/wrangleworks/WranglesPY/issues/1172). Build on existing logging; an optional tracing exporter is not a prerequisite.

Provider references: [PDF inputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/file-inputs), [Images and vision](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/images-vision).
